parts.text:
2
What is a reasonable estimate of the current in an electric kettle that is in use?
A
8 A
B
8 mA
C
8 A
D
8 kA

hints: Notice the kettle is a mains-powered heater in use, so think of its heating power in kilowatts and the mains voltage in volts.
Connect power to current with $P = VI$, so the current must be $I = P/V$ using about $2000 \, \text{W}$ and about $230 \, \text{V}$.
Compare the result in amperes with $8 \, \mu\text{A}$, $8 \, \text{mA}$, $8 \, \text{A}$ and $8 \, \text{kA}$ and reject values a thousand or a million times too small or too large.
walkthrough: Identify the useful estimates: a domestic kettle needs about $2$ to $3 \, \text{kW}$ of heating power and runs on mains voltage of about $230 \, \text{V}$.
State the governing relation for electrical power: $P = VI$, so current is $I = P/V$.

Check the size: microamperes and milliamperes are $10^{-6} \, \text{A}$ and $10^{-3} \, \text{A}$ and far too small, while kiloamperes are $10^{3} \, \text{A}$ and far too large for a $13 \, \text{A}$ domestic plug.
The value near several amperes matches $8 \, \text{A}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: An $8 \, \mu\text{A}$ current is about a million times too small and is typical of tiny sensor or leakage currents, not a heater.

B.explanation: An $8 \, \text{mA}$ current could power a small LED circuit but cannot deliver the kilowatts needed to boil water quickly.

C.explanation: A few kilowatts at about $230 \, \text{V}$ gives $I = P/V$ of several amperes, so about $8 \, \text{A}$ is reasonable.

D.explanation: An $8 \, \text{kA}$ current would mean megawatts of power and would melt domestic wiring and fuses instantly.
